description: Hi, I’m Prakruti, an MS Information Systems student at Northeastern with 7+ years in marketing and storytelling. Wish You Were Here turns the machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space into pen pals for kids: tap a pin, read a postcard in the machine’s own voice, learn what it discovered, then write back. Building solo, but open to anyone who loves design, space history or storytelling.
summary: Wish You Were Here turns the hardware NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space into pen pals for school-age space fans. Kids tap a pin on a Moon or Mars map, read a postcard written in the machine's own voice, and learn what it discovered, whether it still works, and where it rests, with real coordinates and a link to find it on NASA Moon Trek or Mars Trek. They write back, learn how long their reply takes to travel at the speed of light, and collect a stamp for every machine. Fifteen machines are covered, from Surveyor 3 (1967) to Voyager 1, which reaches one light-day from Earth this week. By giving each machine a voice, the project helps young learners remember not just what was left behind, but the science it made possible.
details:
What it does: An interactive storytelling website where 15 machines NASA left behind, including Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 laser mirror, Apollo rovers, Opportunity, Ingenuity and Voyager 1, send kids first-person postcards.

How it works: Kids pick the Moon, Mars or deep space and tap a pin plotted from real landing-site coordinates. They flip a postcard to learn what the machine discovered, why it never came home and whether it still works, then find it on NASA Moon Trek or Mars Trek. They write back, see how long their reply takes at light speed (1.3 seconds to the Moon, up to 22 minutes to Mars, about 24 hours to Voyager 1), and collect stamps. A read-aloud mode and a timeline support younger learners.

Benefits: It turns a list of hardware into memorable stories, builds curiosity and empathy for exploration, and works free on any phone or laptop with no install.

What I hope to achieve: That every young space fan feels these machines are not forgotten, and wants to learn what they discovered.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript; the Web Speech API for read-aloud; GitHub Pages for hosting.
